title: The Relational Model
summary: What a relation actually is under the hood, and why the set-based model beat every alternative that came before it.

slides.markdown:
A **relation** is what you call a "table" when you're being precise: a set of rows, each with the same named columns, drawn from fixed value domains. Every SQL database you've ever used implements this one idea.

Think of a relation like a spreadsheet with rules attached — no two rows identical, no meaningful order, every cell restricted to a domain. Those rules aren't pedantry; they're why the model is provably queryable and why decades of query optimizers can rewrite your SQL safely.

This topic gives you the exact vocabulary interviewers expect — relation, tuple, attribute, domain, schema vs instance — and why this model displaced everything before it.

slides.sectionTitle: The precise vocabulary: relation, tuple, attribute, domain
slides.markdown:
A **relation** is a named set of tuples that all share the same structure — casually, a table. A **tuple** is one row: an ordered set of values, one per attribute — casually, a record. An **attribute** is a named column, and its **domain** is the set of legal values it can hold — `age` might be domain "integers 0-150", not just "any integer."

The layering matters: `Employees` is a relation; `(103, 'Priya', 'Eng')` is a tuple in it; `name` is an attribute; the domain of `name` is "non-empty strings up to some length." A `CHECK` constraint is really just you declaring a domain explicitly instead of leaving it implicit.

Interviewers use this vocabulary to test whether you learned SQL from tutorials or understand the model it implements.

slides.sectionTitle: Schema vs instance, and the closed-world assumption
slides.markdown:
The **schema** is the structure — table names, column names, types, constraints — defined once by `CREATE TABLE`. The **instance** is the actual data sitting in those tables right now, changing with every `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`. The schema is (mostly) stable; the instance churns constantly.

The relational model also assumes a **closed-world assumption**: if a fact isn't in the database, the system treats it as false, not "unknown." Query `WHERE department = 'Legal'` and get zero rows — the model asserts there is no such employee, not "we don't know." This is why `NULL` needs special three-valued logic later: it's the model's one escape hatch for genuinely unknown values.

Interview framing: "schema migration" changes structure; a `DELETE` changes instance — conflating the two is a common junior slip.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a table mapped to relation/tuple/attribute terms
slides.markdown:
![Relation, tuple, attribute, and domain labeled on a sample table](assets/relation-terminology.svg)

The whole grid is the **relation**. Any single row is a **tuple**. Any single column is an **attribute**, and the pool of values it's allowed to hold — say, `{'Eng', 'Sales', 'Legal'}` for `dept` — is its **domain**.

Mapping SQL's informal words to these formal ones is mechanical once you've seen it once: table→relation, row→tuple, column→attribute, column's valid values→domain.

slides.sectionTitle: Why sets: no duplicate rows, no inherent order
slides.markdown:
Mathematically, a relation is a **set** of tuples, and sets have two defining properties that trip people up: no duplicates, and no inherent order. Two identical rows in a true relation collapse to one — `{1, 1, 2}` is just `{1, 2}`. And a set has no first or last element; "the third row" is meaningless unless you explicitly `ORDER BY` something.

SQL tables in practice violate the first property (duplicate rows are allowed unless you add a `UNIQUE`/primary key or use `DISTINCT`) because pure set semantics turned out to be too restrictive for real workloads — but the *design intent* is still set-based, which is why `SELECT *` with no `ORDER BY` gives you rows in whatever order the engine finds convenient, not a guaranteed one.

The practical rule: never depend on row order without an explicit `ORDER BY`, and don't assume the engine will dedupe rows for you.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the model won: physical vs logical data independence
slides.markdown:
Codd's 1970 insight wasn't just "use tables" — it was **data independence**: the guarantee that how data is queried (logically) is decoupled from how it's stored (physically). A DBA can add an index, repartition a table, or switch storage engines, and every existing query keeps working and keeps returning the same answer, just faster or slower.

The older hierarchical and network models (next slide) baked navigation paths — literal pointers between records — into the application code. Reorganize the physical structure and every program that walked those pointers broke. The relational model replaced "tell me how to navigate to the data" with "tell me what data you want" (declarative), and let the engine figure out the path.

This is the property a query optimizer depends on: it's free to pick any execution plan because the *logical* result is guaranteed regardless of the physical one it chooses.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: relational vs the older hierarchical/network models
slides.markdown:
| | Hierarchical (e.g. IMS) | Network (CODASYL) | Relational |
|---|---|---|---|
| Structure | Strict tree — one parent per record | Graph — records can have many parents | Flat tables, related by shared values |
| Access | Navigate the tree from a root | Follow explicit pointer sets | Declarative query — no fixed path |
| Data independence | Low — app code encodes the tree shape | Low — app code walks pointer chains | High — physical layout can change freely |
| Modeling many-to-many | Awkward — trees can't express it directly | Natural — was actually its strength | Natural — via a junction table |

**How to decide (historically):** hierarchical/network models were faster for the one access pattern they were built for, at the cost of every other query being expensive or impossible; relational traded some raw speed for the ability to ask *any* query without rewriting the schema — the trade-off that ultimately won as query flexibility mattered more than raw navigation speed.

slides.sectionTitle: NULL and three-valued logic: the model's escape hatch
slides.markdown:
`NULL` represents "unknown" or "not applicable," and it breaks ordinary two-valued (true/false) logic. `NULL = NULL` evaluates to `UNKNOWN`, not `TRUE` — two unknown values aren't necessarily equal to each other. This is why `WHERE column = NULL` never matches anything; you need `IS NULL`.

Three-valued logic (`TRUE`/`FALSE`/`UNKNOWN`) then propagates: `UNKNOWN AND TRUE` is `UNKNOWN`, and a `WHERE` clause only keeps rows where the condition is `TRUE` — `UNKNOWN` rows are silently dropped, which surprises people debugging "missing" rows in a report.

Staff-level nuance: aggregate functions like `COUNT(column)` skip `NULL`s, but `COUNT(*)` doesn't — a subtle source of off-by-N bugs in analytics queries that nobody notices until the numbers don't reconcile.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: treating row order or physical layout as meaningful
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This query always comes back in insertion order, so I don't need `ORDER BY`."

**Why it's wrong:** relations are sets — the model gives zero guarantees about row order. What you're observing is an artifact of the current storage layout and query plan: heap scan order, an index the optimizer happened to pick, or parallel workers merging results. Add an index, upgrade the database version, let the table grow past a size threshold that flips the plan, or just run the same query on a replica, and the "always" order can silently change.

**Correct model:** if order matters to the application — pagination, "most recent first," display order — say so explicitly with `ORDER BY`. Anything else is relying on an implementation detail the engine is free to break without notice, and it will, usually in production after a version upgrade.

slides.sectionTitle: In production: how a row actually sits on disk
slides.markdown:
The logical model says "a set of tuples," but a working engineer should know the physical reality: most OLTP engines (Postgres, MySQL/InnoDB) store rows in fixed-size **pages** (commonly 8KB or 16KB) inside a **heap** (Postgres) or clustered around the primary key (InnoDB). A `SELECT` without an index means scanning every page — a **full table scan** — which is why the logical/physical split matters practically: adding an index changes nothing about what a query returns, only how many pages it has to touch.

This is also where `VACUUM` (Postgres) or page fragmentation (InnoDB) comes from: `UPDATE`/`DELETE` don't always rewrite in place, leaving dead tuples that the engine has to reclaim later — a purely physical concern the logical model deliberately hides from you.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: what a relation-based engine can actually do
slides.markdown:
Concretely: a well-indexed relational table can serve a primary-key lookup in **sub-millisecond** time regardless of whether the table has 10 thousand or 10 billion rows, because an index turns "scan the set" into "walk a B-tree in O(log n)." Without an index, that same lookup degrades to O(n) — a 10-million-row full scan on spinning disk can take seconds; on SSD, still tens to hundreds of milliseconds.

That gap — indexed O(log n) vs unindexed O(n) — is the single most common root cause behind "the database got slow" incidents, and it's a direct, practical consequence of the logical/physical independence from slide 6: the query didn't change, only the physical access path did.
